Appeals Consolidated;
Petitions for Stay Denied
Oregon Natural Desert Association and Western Watersheds Project, (collectively
referred to as ONDA) have appealed from and petitioned for a stay of five final decisions each
2

OR-030-05-01 through 06
dated July 7, 2005 (Final Decisions), renewing grazing permits in the Louse Canyon
Geographic Management Area (LCGMA). The Final Decisions were issued by the Acting
Field Manager, Jordan Field Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM or Respondent).
Kimble Wilkinson Ranches (hereafter Wilkinson) has separately appealed and petitioned for a
stay of one of the Final Decisions renewing its grazing privileges in the LCGMA.
The Final Decisions provide for renewal of five 10-year grazing permits to the
permittees in the LCGMA. The Decisions are all based on environmental assessment # OR
030-04-013 (EA). In the EA, BLM analyzes seven management alternatives for the roughly
520,000-acre LCGMA which is located in the southeastern corner of Oregon bordering both
Idaho and Nevada. The Final Decisions authorize continued grazing in the LCGMA of
approximately 37,010 animal unit months (AUMs). Additionally, the Final Decisions
authorize range improvement projects including vegetation treatments on 3,500 acres, troughs,
pipelines, and the construction of 58 miles of fence (EA at 74).
Based on the EA, the Acting Field Manager issued a Findings of No Significant Impact
(FONSI) within each Final Decision. In the FONSIs he concluded that the proposed actions
were not likely to significantly impact the human environment, considering the factors set
forth at 40 C.F.R. § 1508.27, and thus that BLM was not required by section 102(2)(C) of the
National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C)
(2000), to first prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS). In the EA the Acting Field
Manager also concluded that the proposed actions conform with the 2001 Southeastern
Oregon Resource Management Plan and Final Environmental Impact Statement (SEORMP
FEIS), BLM’s applicable land use planning documents (EA at 3).
Appeals Consolidated
Although ONDA has raised all of its grounds for appeal in a single document, and
despite ONDA characterizing that document as a single appeal, the document, in fact,
constitutes five appeals because ONDA is challenging five different decisions. Three of the
decisions address grazing management for the Louse Canyon Community Allotment, which
Wilkinson grazes with two other permittees. One decision was issued to each of the
permittees and both ONDA and Wilkinson have appealed the decision addressing Wilkinson’s
grazing privileges. The other two decisions pertain to grazing in different allotments.
On August 31, 2005, Respondent filed a motion to consolidate ONDA’s five appeals
and the Wilkinson appeal. On September 12, 2005, ONDA filed a response indicating that it
did not oppose consolidation. On September 14, 2005, Wilkinson filed a response objecting
to consolidation of its appeal with the five ONDA appeals. In that response Wilkinson also
characterizes ONDA’s filing as a single appeal and argues:
Even though both appeals concern the final decision[s] involving the Louse
3

OR-030-05-01 through 06
Canyon Geographic Management Area, the scope of the appeals is entirely
different. * * *
Wilkinson’s appeal does not request an EIS or elimination of continued
livestock grazing. Wilkinson is concerned about some of the proposed grazing
schedules and the AUM allotments, among other things. Accordingly,
Wilkinson’s appeal does not come close to the scope of the ONDA appeal.
Consolidating these appeals will require Wilkinson to participate in
discussions about numerous unrelated, complex issues forcing an expense of
significant time and expense. Allowing these appeals to proceed separately
through the system will be the most economical for Wilkinson ranches and
provide for the most streamlined approach to the Wilkinson appeal without
complicating the appeal with the numerous, intricate issues from ONDA’s
appeal.
(Id. at 1-2).
While the scope of the appeals may be different, consolidation is nevertheless
appropriate for several reasons. First, ONDA and Wilkinson have both appealed the decision
addressing Wilkinson=s grazing privileges in the Louse Canyon Community Allotment. At a
minimum, those appeals must be consolidated to avoid the potential of conflicting decisions
being issued on appeal regarding the same BLM decision.
Second, ONDA and Wilkinson have both raised certain issues, including that the Final
Decision regarding Wilkinson=s privileges will fail to improve conditions on the Louse
Canyon Community Allotment and that BLM violated NEPA and § 302(a) of the Federal
Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA), as amended, 43 U.S.C. ' 1732(a)
(2000). Third, all five Final Decisions, and the three decisions pertaining to Louse Canyon
Community Allotment in particular, appear to be interdependent parts of a coordinated grazing
management strategy based upon many common facts and analyses in the EA and SEORMP
FEIS.
Under the circumstances, conducting separate proceedings may result in inconsistent
decisions or the creation of an altered grazing scheme for the area which has not been
analyzed by BLM, the agency with the expertise and responsibility to do so in the first
instance. Further, economy of administration and the overall convenience of the parties and
witnesses dictates that the matters should be consolidated. Accordingly, the appeals are
hereby consolidated.
Petitions for Stay Denied
To prevail on their petitions, Appellants must show, in accordance with 43 C.F.R.
§ 4.471(c)(2), sufficient justification based on the relative harm to the parties if the stay is
4

OR-030-05-01 through 06
granted or denied, the likelihood of Appellants’ success on the merits, the likelihood of
immediate and irreparable harm if the stay is not granted, and whether the public interest
favors the granting of the stays. The parties seeking the stays bear the burden of
demonstrating that they are warranted under each of the regulatory criteria. See 43 C.F.R.
§ 4.471(d); Oregon Natural Resources Council, 148 IBLA 186, 188 (1993).
To achieve success on the merits, Appellants must meet their burden to demonstrate,
by a preponderance of the evidence, that the Final Decisions are unreasonable or do not
substantially comply with the provisions of the Federal grazing regulations found at 43 C.F.R.
part 4100. See 43 C.F.R. § 4.480(b); Eason v. BLM, 127 IBLA 259, 262 (1993). A BLM
decision may be regarded as arbitrary, capricious, or inequitable only where it is not supported
by any rational basis. Wayne D. Klump v. BLM, 124 IBLA 176, 182 (1992). Based upon a
preliminary review of the record and pleadings, and as more fully discussed below, I find that
Appellants have failed to meet their burden of showing that stays are warranted under each of
the four regulatory criteria.
Likelihood of Success on the Merits
As more fully discussed below, neither Appellant has shown a likelihood of success on
the merits of their challenges to the Final Decisions.
A. ONDA’s Argument that the BLM Must Prepare an EIS in Order to Take the
Requisite “Hard Look” at the Environmental Consequences of this Massive
Rangeland Project.
In its appeal and petition for stay ONDA argues that the Final Decisions will have a
significant effect on the environment and, therefore, that BLM must prepare an EIS, rather
than an EA, to evaluate the Final Decisions, ONDA writes:
Because the EA and final decision cover well over a half million acres of
public land, could take up to a decade or more to implement, include broad-
scale rangeland projects, involve grazing management decisions for areas
determined to be in violation of applicable rangeland health standards, affect
populations of declining sensitive species, and would take place within both
designated WSAs and non-WSA roadless areas with inventoried and
documented wilderness values, this project requires an EIS rather than an EA.
(ONDA’s appeal and petition for stay (hereafter “ONDA Appeal”) at 4).
BLM counters ONDA’s argument that an EIS is necessary by, among other things,
pointing out that the EA is tiered to the SEORMP FEIS:
5

OR-030-05-01 through 06
The [EA] is tiered to and incorporates by reference * * * the [SEORMP FEIS],
which entirely encompasses the area of the LCGMA. In addition, the
[SEORMP FEIS] fully discloses and discusses impacts that may or may not be
significant, including the effects of projects like pipelines, fences, and of
grazing system changes in a broad landscape context over a relatively long
period of time. Since the LCGMA EA does not include any specific projects or
grazing systems that fall beyond the scope of those already discussed in the
[SEORMP FEIS] or that, after applying mitigation, would significantly affect
the quality of the human environment, BLM reached the conclusion that no EIS
is necessary and issued a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) for each of
the proposed grazing permit renewals.
(Respondent’s response to ONDA’s stay request (hereinafter “Response to ONDA”) at 9
(quoting Final Decisions at 4 )).
ONDA argues that BLM cannot properly tier the actions in the Final Decisions to the
SEORMP FEIS because BLM has indicated that: “the [SEORMP FEIS] was designed to set
broad goals and objectives for resource management, with specific strategies and more
detailed analyses occurring in the future at the site-specific project stage * * * (ONDA Appeal
at 5).
In Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 123 IBLA 302, 306 (1992) the Interior Board
of Land Appeals (the Board) explained that:
[40 C.F.R. § 1502.20] allow[s] an EA to be tiered to a previously completed
EIS. The provisions at 40 CFR 1502.20 explicitly discuss moving from a
broad EIS to a subsequent EA. Similarly, the definition of tiering at 40 CFR
1508.28 states that tiering is appropriate when moving from an EIS to a “site-
specific statement or analysis.” See In re Humphy Mountain Timber Sale, 88
IBLA 7, 8 (1985).
The SEORMP FEIS identifies the types of grazing programs and projects that will
occur in the LCGMA. The SEORMP FEIS also includes overarching restrictions,
descriptions, and mitigation measures governing implementation of grazing programs and
projects in the LCGMA. The SEORMP FEIS even reaches beyond broad generalities and,
among other things, identifies the type of pipe which will typically be used for water projects
and explains how that pipe will be buried or laid (SEORMP FEIS, Appendix S at 389-93).
The EA tiers to the SEORMP FEIS and identifies site-specific actions that will be
taken in various allotments and pastures of the LCGMA. Beginning at page 74 of the EA,
BLM explains specifically how grazing will be managed in each pasture of the LCGMA. This
portion of the EA also specifically describes projects that will be developed in each pasture,
6

OR-030-05-01 through 06
including a description of how and where those projects will be implemented and the
mitigation measures which will be used to reduce their impacts to insignificance.
Nonetheless, ONDA argues that the Final Decisions require a separate EIS. For
purposes of evaluating whether BLM should have conducted a separate EIS for the Final
Decisions, the salient question is whether implementation of the Final Decisions will result in
any significant impacts, not mitigated to insignificance, which were not analyzed in the
SEORMP FEIS. If the answer to that question is yes, it is necessary that those impacts be
considered in a separate EIS. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 123 IBLA at 306; see also
Blue Mountain Biodiversity Project, 139 IBLA 258, 266 (1997).
ONDA argues that BLM has failed to consider certain significant impacts. For
example, ONDA argues that BLM has failed to consider the impacts of fencing and other
projects in terms of weed infestation and the effects of those projects on potential future
wilderness designation (ONDA Appeal at 7). BLM has concluded that weed infestation is a
relatively small problem in the LCGMA, with only traces of various weed species having been
identified in the area (Final Decisions at 52; LCGMA, 2002 Standard for Rangeland Health
Evaluation (hereinafter “Evaluation”) at 26).
BLM has considered the projects authorized through the Final Decisions in terms of
weed infestation. With regard to water troughs, pipelines, and vegetative treatments, BLM
explains that the weed invasion is not expected to occur as a result of these projects because of
the low incidence of exotic species in the LCGMA (EA at 74-77). Specific impacts expected
by BLM from the authorized fencing projects include denuded vegetation along livestock
trails adjacent to fence lines and short-term crushed vegetation in the vicinity of new fence
construction (EA at 76). While BLM does not specifically state that it does not expect weed
invasion to result from fence construction, the EA and the Evaluation clearly indicate that
weed invasion is not a significant impact which is expected to result from construction of any
of the range projects.
BLM has also considered the impact of the Final Decisions on any future wilderness
designations. In the EA at pages 199-200, BLM identifies projects which will be constructed
within Wilderness Study Areas (WSAs). BLM concludes that impacts associated with these
projects are outweighed by the enhancement of wilderness values which will result from the
projects. Accordingly, BLM makes a finding in the EA that implementation of the preferred
alternative will meet the non-impairment criteria of BLM’s policy on WSA management as set
forth in the Interim Management Policy and Guidelines for lands under Wilderness Review H-
8550-1.
At minimum, ONDA has a burden to raise substantial questions as to whether the
Final Decisions will have a significant affect. Idaho Sporting Congress v. Thomas, 137 F.3d
1146, 1149 (9th Cir. 1998). ONDA speculates that the Final Decisions will have significant
7

OR-030-05-01 through 06
impacts not considered in the SEORMP FEIS or not mitigated to insignificance through the
identified mitigation measures but fails to support these assertions with adequate evidence or
to identify any consequential gaps in BLM’s analysis.
BLM’s analysis, description, and discussion in the SEORMP FEIS and EA evidence
the fact that BLM has taken a hard look at the actions identified in the Final Decisions and
their associated impacts in reaching the conclusion that the Final Decisions will not result in
any significant impacts beyond those considered and discussed in the SEORMP FEIS.
Accordingly, I find that ONDA has not met its burden to demonstrate a likelihood of success
on the merits of its argument that BLM should have prepared an EIS for the Final Decisions.
B. ONDA’s Argument that BLM ‘s Refusal to Analyze Potential Effects to the
Wilderness Resources Violates NEPA.
On February 6, 2004, ONDA submitted to BLM its own wilderness inventory which
identifies lands, including some in the LCGMA, it recommends for WSA designation. ONDA
argues that BLM violated both NEPA and FLPMA by refusing to consider designation of
ONDA’s identified lands as WSAs and by failing to consider wilderness values and potential
impacts to wilderness resources in the EA (ONDA Appeal at 8-9).
With regard to those lands in the LCGMA that are designated as WSAs, BLM states
that it has considered their wilderness values in the EA and determined that the proposed
action is consistent with BLM’s policy on WSA management as set forth in the Interim
Management Policy and Guidelines for lands under Wilderness Review H-8550-1 (Final
Decisions at 8; EA at 199-200).
With regard to ONDA’s recommended WSA lands, BLM argues that consideration of
new WSAs is beyond the scope of its EA and Final Decisions (Response to ONDA at 12-13;
Final Decisions at 8). Respondent explains that the wilderness review process was completed
for Oregon on July 22, 1992, when the President transmitted his official wilderness
recommendations to Congress identifying WSAs for the state of Oregon in accordance with 43
U.S.C. § 1782. Respondent argues that lands not recommended as WSAs are not subject to
FLMPA’s non-impairment requirement. Colorado Environmental Coalition, 161 IBLA 386,
393 (2004).
The Board has repeatedly rejected challenges to BLM decisions authorizing uses on
non-WSAs based on allegations that the non-WSAs should be designated as WSAs and that
the authorized uses might impair wilderness characteristics on those lands. See Id. In
Colorado Environmental Coalition, the Board noted that “[t]he time for taking appeals from
the inventory decisions [made in the early 1980's] had long since passed, and * * * found that
the doctrine of administrative finality precluded appellants from challenging those decisions
by protesting actions taken by BLM to administer the land for other purposes.” Id. at 393-94.
8

OR-030-05-01 through 06
While BLM lacks authority to designate new WSAs or manage areas excluded from
further wilderness study as if they are, or may become, wilderness areas, it does retain
authority to consider wilderness characteristics and manage such lands using special
protections to protect those characteristics. Id. at 395-96. Indeed, BLM has the duty to
“prepare and maintain on a continuing basis an inventory of all public lands and their resource
and other values * * *.” 43 U.S.C. § 1711(a).
ONDA argues that many conditions have changed in the area since BLM conducted its
original wilderness inventory and that BLM should have considered those changes in the EA.
However, BLM’s responsibility to maintain on a continuing basis an inventory of all public
lands is limited to the land use planning process and does not extend to project level decision-
making. This position is supported by BLM Instruction Memorandum (IM) 2003-274 (Sept.
29, 2003), which interprets a settlement agreement reached in the case of State of Utah, et al.
v. Norton, et al., Civ. No. 96-C-870 B (D. Utah Apr. 14, 2003), as having the following effect
upon proposals by wilderness advocates:
BLM will continue to manage public lands according to existing land use plans
while new information (e.g., in the form of new resource assessments,
wilderness inventory areas or ‘citizen’s proposals’) is being considered in a
land use planning effort. During the planning process and concluding with the
actions after the planning process, BLM will not manage those lands under a
congressionally designated non-impairment standard, nor manage them as if
they are or may become congressionally designated wilderness areas, but
through the planning process BLM may manage them using special protections
to protect wilderness characteristics.
(IM 2003-274 at 2). The Board has characterized this position as reflective of the statutory
requirements and has held that alternative uses of the land need not be considered anew each
time BLM decides to undertake an activity. Colorado Environmental Coalition, 161 IBLA at
396.
Nevertheless, BLM did address ONDA’s wilderness inventory in the Final Decisions
at pages 8-9 and provided a rational explanation for why it did not consider a new wilderness
review as being within the scope of the EA. Consequently, ONDA has not demonstrated a
sufficient likelihood of success on its claim that BLM violated NEPA or FLPMA by failing to
discuss in detail wilderness values and the impacts to wilderness resources beyond its
discussion of impacts to existing WSAs and finding of non-impairment.
9

OR-030-05-01 through 06
C. ONDA’s Argument that BLM Failed to Take a “Hard Look” at Potential
Effects to Sage Grouse Populations and Habitat Throughout the Louse Canyon
GMA.
ONDA argues that BLM has failed to consider significant impacts to sage grouse and
other wildlife species and failed to establish baseline information against which impacts can
be measured. ONDA also contends that BLM has failed to consider cumulative impacts to
wildlife, that the Final Decisions are inconsistent with the SEORMP FEIS, and that the EA
does not adequately address the fact that approximately 50% of the streams in the LCGMA are
not meeting the applicable standard for functioning riparian wetlands.
ONDA’s assertions are not born out by the record. At pages 12-16 the EA addresses
the issue of managing the LCGMA in conformance with appropriate BLM guidance on sage
grouse conservation. BLM identifies impacts to sage grouse and explains how those impacts
will be mitigated to insignificance. For example, BLM explains that new fencing will be
temporarily flagged to help prevent collisions with sage grouse and other wildlife species (EA
at 16).
Available wildlife and rangeland baseline data for the LCGMA is discussed in the EA,
Evaluation, and in the SEORMP FEIS. See EA at 12-17, 35, Evaluation chapter 2 generally,
SEORMP FEIS Volume 1 Chapter 2 at 71-79. Additionally, the EA discusses monitoring,
including monitoring of sage grouse, that will occur in the LCGMA at pages 12-17, 34-35.
The EA explains and identifies impacts of grazing management under the preferred
alternative on wildlife species in the LCGMA, including sage grouse, and how the actions
authorized in the Final Decisions are in conformance with the SEORMP FEIS. Discussion
and analysis of impacts to wildlife, mitigation for those impacts, and conformance with
applicable planning documents, including the SEORMP FEIS, is evident throughout the EA.
See EA at 4-16, 57-58, 18-19, 150-186; see also Final Decisions at 12-13.
ONDA’s assertion that BLM has failed to address non-functioning riparian conditions
is not supported by the record. The EA addresses impacts to soils, water resources, and
riparian areas for the preferred alternative at pages 133-139. See also Final Decisions at 27-
36. In fact, one of the guiding principals behind the grazing schedule authorized through the
Final Decisions, as well as many of the various authorized rangeland projects, including
exclosure fencing, division fencing, and pipelines carrying water to troughs away from
protected riparian sources, is to help move toward improved riparian conditions in the
LCGMA (EA at 133-135).
While ONDA has asserted a failure on BLM’s part to consider impacts on the above-
described resources and to various environmental values, the record indicates otherwise. The
record evidences a hard look by BLM at potential impacts to wildlife and riparian resources,
10

OR-030-05-01 through 06
including consideration of baseline information. Additionally, the EA indicates that BLM has
provided for future monitoring to determine if management strategies implemented through
the Final Decisions are achieving BLM’s goals of improving ecological conditions while
continuing commodity production in the LCGMA.
ONDA has the burden to do more than request additional information and reiterate its
differences of opinion with BLM regarding outcomes that it believes will result from
management under the Final Decisions. See In re Stratton Hog Timber Sale, 160 IBLA 329,
332 (2004); see also Edward C. Faulkner, 164 IBLA 204, 209 (2004). To succeed in arguing
that BLM has failed to take a hard look at impacts to sage grouse and other wildlife species,
ONDA must affirmatively demonstrate either an error of law or fact through objective
evidence. See id., and cases cited therein. ONDA has not met this burden or demonstrated a
likelihood that it will be able to do so.
D. ONDA’s Argument that the BLM Refused to Consider the Suitability of
Livestock Grazing at Continued Levels.
ONDA argues that BLM should conduct a suitability study regarding grazing in the
LCGMA. However, BLM has addressed and considered this issue in the context of the
SEORMP FEIS, where it evaluated grazing as an appropriate use for lands within the
LCGMA. In response to ONDA’s argument BLM writes:
The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934, as amended, allowed for the establishment of
grazing districts where the lands contained within were chiefly valuable for
grazing and raising forage crops. Public lands contained within the LCGMA,
which are the subject of ONDA’s protests, are located within established
grazing districts. BLM has more recently addressed these areas through the
[SEORMP FEIS] land use planning process, and as part of this process decided
to provide for a sustained level of livestock grazing consistent with other
resource objectives and public land use allocations. The LCGMA process and
this decision accomplish this.
(Final Decisions at 14-15).
In Oregon Natural Resources Council Action, et al., 148 IBLA 186, 190 (1999), the
Board explained that:
[a]n RMP (or conforming MFP) is a document that establishes, “[a]mong
other things, allowable resource uses (either singly or in combination) and
related levels of production or use to be maintained.” *** Thus, whether to
allow grazing and at what levels is clearly beyond the scope and an activity
level plan such as an AMP.
11

OR-030-05-01 through 06
(quoting Headwaters, Inc., 101 IBLA 234, 237 (1988)). Accordingly, BLM is not obligated to
revisit the issue of whether grazing should occur on the allotments in the LCGMA as part of
its analysis in the EA.
ONDA also argues that BLM has failed to consider an adequate range of authorized
AUMs in the EA. Again, this argument is not born out by the record. BLM analyzed four
different alternatives which would have reduced authorized AUMs in the LCGMA, with
reductions ranging from 17% to 79% (EA at Table 1). This range of alternatives meets the
applicable standard which is referred to as the “rule of reason.” In Wade Patrick Stout, et al.,
153 IBLA 13, 21 (2000), the Board described the rule of reason standard as follows: “In
determining whether an EA promotes informed decision making, a ‘rule of reason’ will be
employed. The query is whether the EA contains a ‘reasonably thorough discussion of the
significant aspects of the probable environmental consequences’ of the proposed action and
the alternatives thereto.” Id. at 21. (quoting State of California v. Block, 609 F.2d 753, 761
(9th Cir. 1982)).
Finally, ONDA argues that BLM failed to explain how the Final Decisions will comply
with BLM’s statewide drought policy and that the failure to do so constitutes an unlawful gap
in BLM’s NEPA analysis (ONDA Appeal at 16). Concerning drought, in the Final Decisions
BLM explains that:
BLM does not base long-term planning and development of grazing systems on
less-than-normal periods of moisture. Therefore, drought conditions do not
need to be addressed in documents which issue grazing permits. However,
BLM does consider drought conditions, as well as other circumstances that
limit forage production, in annual grazing authorizations.
(Final Decisions at 16).
If BLM’s position regarding drought is somehow legally insufficient, ONDA has not
demonstrated that deficiency. ONDA has not provided a statewide policy that the EA or Final
Decisions violate. Moreover, ONDA cannot show error in the EA by merely reiterating
arguments which have already been adequately addressed by BLM. See Edward C. Faulkner,
164 IBLA at 210. Accordingly, ONDA has not demonstrated a likelihood of success
regarding the preceding arguments.
E. ONDA’s Argument that BLM’s Reliance on Defunct Rangeland Projects, and
Decision to Construct Even More Projects, is further Evidence of Arbitrary
and Capricious Decisionmaking.
ONDA argues that the EA fails to consider the cumulative impacts of existing
operating and defunct rangeland projects. ONDA avers that there are over 200 existing
12

OR-030-05-01 through 06
projects in the Campbell Star Valley Community Allotment alone and that only 25% of those
projects are in working condition.
The record does not support the assertion that BLM ignored existing and inoperative
rangeland projects in the EA. See Evaluation, Chap. 6 at 16-24, Table 6; EA at 8-9, 137; Final
Decisions at 25-26. Furthermore, ONDA cannot simply assert that existing and defunct
rangeland projects have significant impacts. ONDA has a burden to demonstrate by objective
evidence that the projects are likely to have a significant impact. Edward C. Faulkner, 164
IBLA at 209. ONDA has not offered adequate evidence supporting its assertions of
significant impacts due to defunct rangeland projects or of a likelihood of success regarding its
argument that the EA is deficient or that BLM has acted arbitrarily or capriciously.
F. ONDA’s argument that BLM’s Reliance on Monitoring that is Not Certain to
Occur and Based on Almost No Quantitative Measurements is Arbitrary and
Capricious.
ONDA takes issue with BLM’s monitoring strategy primarily because it employs
qualitative, rather than quantitative, measures. However, BLM has had success using a non-
quantitative system in the Trout Creek/Oregon Canyon Mountain pastures and has adequately
explained its monitoring regime and the rationale therefor (Final Decision at 23-24; EA at 34-
35). Further, that regime does include a quantitative measure to trigger removal of cattle
from riparian pastures. Under the Final Decisions, cattle are removed from riparian areas
when utilization of woody species reaches 30% (EA at 35).
ONDA objects to BLM’s monitoring strategy and identifies monitoring approaches it
would prefer. However, ONDA fails to explain how, or demonstrate why, BLM’s monitoring
regime lacks a rational foundation. ONDA’s difference of opinion and preference for
qualitative data does not demonstrate error in BLM’s EA or Final Decisions. Coy Brown, 115
IBLA 347, 355-57 (1990). ONDA has the burden to show error in BLM’s monitoring regime.
This burden extends beyond reiterating arguments raised in its protest to the proposed
decisions which have already been adequately considered and addressed by the decision
maker. Edward C. Faulkner, 164 IBLA at 210. Here, BLM has addressed ONDA’s concerns
noting that it has had success using qualitative systems elsewhere and that monitoring will
employ some quantitative measures. Accordingly, I find that ONDA is unlikely to prevail
regarding its monitoring arguments.
G. ONDA’s Argument that the BLM Failed to Adequately Analyze the Cumulative
Impacts of the Proposed Action.
ONDA argues that BLM has failed to consider the cumulative impacts of the proposed
actions. This argument is not supported by the record. BLM has considered the cumulative

impacts of the proposed actions in the EA throughout the document. See EA at 4-20, 122-
139, 150-186, 208-210; see also Final Decisions at 25-26.
Moreover, ONDA has failed to meet its burden of demonstrating the possibility of a
particular cumulative impact that BLM failed to consider and of establishing that such impact
would be significant. See San Juan Citizens Alliance et al., 129 IBLA 1, 11 (1994). ONDA
has not shown that, because of geographic proximity and/or other reasons, there is a likely
interaction between other activities and the authorized actions which may result in an
enhanced or modified impact that BLM did not consider. See Klamath Siskiyou Wildlands
Center, 157 IBLA 332, 340 (2002). Accordingly, I find that ONDA is unlikely to succeed on
the merits of its argument that BLM’s cumulative impacts analysis is deficient.
H. Wilkinson’s Argument that Grazing Management under the Final Decision Will
Result in Inadequate Water for its Cattle, Reduced Aums, and Degraded
Resource Conditions.
Wilkinson asserts that grazing management under the Final Decision will result in
inadequate water for its cattle, reduced AUMs, and degraded resource conditions (Wilkinson
Appeal at 8, 13-14 ). Wilkinson supports these assertions with a report written by Stephen G.
Leonard, a certified range management consultant, and the affidavit of Conrad Bateman, a
range consultant and a retired range conservationist who worked for BLM for over 30 years.
The affidavit and report include photographs and field observations made by the consultants as
well as a proposed grazing management system that, according to Bateman, would meet
BLM’s objectives and be less onerous on Wilkinson’s ranching operations. To succeed on the
merits, Wilkinson must show that the Final Decision is not supported by any rational basis.
Wayne D. Klump 124 IBLA at 182.
To show that BLM’s Final Decision is incorrect Wilkinson must show positive
evidence of error on BLM’s part. See Ross James v. BLM, 152 IBLA 273 (2000). Mere
differences of opinion between BLM’s experts and Wilkinson’s experts regarding rangeland
conditions and effective rangeland management are insufficient to show error in BLM’s Final
Decision. Beard Oil Co., et al., 99 IBLA 40, 45 (1987); see also Coy Brown, 115 IBLA 347,
355-57 (1990). Accordingly, Wilkinson has not demonstrated a likelihood of success on the
merits.
Balance of Harm and Irreparable Harm
Neither Appellant has demonstrated that the balance of harm weighs in favor of
granting a stay. If a stay were granted, grazing in the LCGMA would continue under the terms
in effect immediately prior to issuance of the Final Decisions. 43 C.F.R. § 4160.3(d). These
terms are interim management guidelines which were established because allotments in the
LCGMA were failing to meet applicable standards for rangeland health. Under those
14

OR-030-05-01 through 06
guidelines grazing was resulting in continued resource conflicts (EA at 3, Evaluation at 2), and
ONDA has challenge those guidelines in federal court as being inadequate stop-gap measures.
If a stay is denied BLM can proceed with implementation of the Final Decisions. The
Final Decisions and accompanying EA, SEORMP FEIS and Evaluation evidence a
conscientious hard look at the competing uses and available resources in the LCGMA.
Through the Final Decisions, BLM implements land management that balances competing
values and interest. The EA and other planning documents make a strong case that
management under the Final Decisions will help the LCGMA meet BLM’s goals of achieving
“a high level of natural resource protection and improvement in ecological conditions while
providing commodity production.” (EA at 40)
Wilkinson generally avers that the Final Decision governing its grazing privileges will
result in negative economic impacts to its ranching operations, including interference with its
crop harvesting activities. Wilkinson argues that the grazing schedule outlined in that
decision requires it to move cattle at the same time it currently harvests crops. However,
Wilkinson fails to explain in detail, and substantiate with evidence, why and to what degree
alleged negative economic impacts will result (Wilkinson appeal and petition for stay at 14;
see also Affidavit of George Wilkinson at ¶ 8). This failure to provide detail and evidence of
detrimental economic impacts is of particular concern because Wilkinson’s authorized AUMs,
6202, are not reduced under the terms of the Final Decision (Respondent’s response to
Wilkinson at 4; see also Wilkinson’s Final Decision at 107).
Where BLM is managing over 500,000 acres of public lands with tens of thousands of
authorized AUMs allocated among multiple graziers, inconveniences, or even negative
economic impacts, to individual graziers are bound to occur. Without detailed description,
evidence and data, Wilkinson’s allegations of negative economic impact cannot support a
petition for stay. See Oregon Natural Resources Council Action 148 IBLA at 188.
Accordingly, I find that Appellants have failed to show that the balance of harm
weighs in favor of granting a stay. Additionally, I find that Appellants have failed to
demonstrate that irreparable harm is likely to result if a stay is not granted.
The Public Interest
I do not believe that the public interest would be served by granting a stay under the
facts of this proceeding. The record evidences a conscientious and thorough effort on BLM’s
part in managing the LCGMA consistently with NEPA and FLPMA. BLM has made a
convincing case that management under the Final Decisions will result in sustained
commodity production and improved ecological conditions. Forestalling BLM’s effort to
achieve these goals based on the evidence and arguments presented to this point, would not
serve the public interest.
